setup: A USD 200m portfolio holds a 1-year and a 5-year bond, USD 100m each. Average maturity is 3 years; Macaulay duration is 2.768 years. Zero-coupon VaR%: 2-year $0.9868\%$, 3-year $1.4841\%$. Principal mapping reads VaR% at the average maturity; duration mapping interpolates it at the duration.
ask: Switching from principal mapping to duration mapping, the portfolio VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Duration (2.768 years) sits below the 3-year average maturity, and VaR% rises with maturity, so the duration VaR% must be lower than 1.4841%.

options.label: Stays the same
options.why: Same notional, but a different VaR% is applied: 1.3687% at 2.768 years against 1.4841% at 3 years.

takeaway: Principal > duration > cash-flow (diversified) VaR: each method adds information and trims apparent risk.

setup: Duration mapping. A USD 200m bond portfolio has duration 2.768 years. Zero-coupon VaR%: 2-year $0.9868\%$, 3-year $1.4841\%$. Interpolate VaR% at the duration and apply it to the notional.
ask: Duration-mapping VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.76m
options.why: Kept only the interpolation step, $(1.4841 - 0.9868)\times 0.768 = 0.382\%$, and forgot to add the 2-year base of 0.9868%.

options.label: ≈ USD 7.6m
options.why: Multiplied by the duration a second time. The VaR% is already the figure for a 2.768-year zero, so there is nothing left to scale.

options.label: ≈ USD 270m
options.why: Applied 1.3687 as a decimal instead of a percent. VaR larger than the whole USD 200m portfolio is the giveaway.

takeaway: Mapped VaR on a USD 200m bond book is a percent or two of notional: low millions, never hundreds.

setup: Cash-flow mapping of the same two-bond portfolio. The 1-year bucket holds PV USD 104.83m with VaR% $0.4696\%$; the 5-year bucket holds PV USD 81.88m with VaR% $2.4261\%$. Each bucket's contribution to undiversified VaR is $x \times V$.
ask: Which bucket contributes more to undiversified VaR?

options.label: The 1-year bucket
options.why: It has the larger PV, but its VaR% is about a fifth of the 5-year figure. PV is only 1.3 times larger, so the VaR% gap wins.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The VaR% gap (about 5×) swamps the PV gap (about 1.3×). The 5-year bucket carries roughly four times the risk.

takeaway: In cash-flow mapping, the long bucket's VaR% dominates even when its PV is smaller.

setup: You sold a $6 \times 12$ FRA on USD 100m, mapped as a 180-day leg of $x_1 = -97.991$ (VaR% 0.1629%) and a 360-day leg of $x_2 = +97.991$ (VaR% 0.4696%). The two rates have correlation 0.79. Diversified variance $= (x_1V_1)^2 + (x_2V_2)^2 + 2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$.
ask: The cross term $2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$ is:

options.label: Positive, so it adds to VaR
options.why: That would need both legs on the same side. Here $x_1 < 0$ and $x_2 > 0$, so with $\rho > 0$ the product is negative and the legs hedge each other.

options.label: Roughly zero
options.why: The correlation is 0.79, far from zero, and the cross term (−0.116) is about half the size of the squared long leg (0.212).

takeaway: Opposite-signed legs + positive correlation = negative cross term: the FRA's two legs largely hedge each other.

setup: A sold $6 \times 12$ FRA maps to a short 180-day leg (risk $x_1V_1 = -0.160$) and a long 360-day leg (risk $x_2V_2 = +0.460$), in USD millions. At a correlation of 0.79 the diversified VaR is 0.348. The correlation between the 180-day and 360-day rates now rises to 0.95.
ask: The FRA's diversified VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: True for two same-signed exposures. These legs have opposite signs, so higher correlation makes the hedge tighter.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Diversified VaR depends on the correlation through the cross term $2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$, which changes here. Only the undiversified sum (0.620) ignores it.

takeaway: Higher correlation raises VaR for same-sign exposures but lowers it for hedged (opposite-sign) ones.

setup: A 1-year forward to buy EUR 100m for USD 126.5m maps into three legs, each with present value USD 122.911m: EUR spot (monthly VaR% $4.5381\%$), a long 1-year EUR bill ($0.1396\%$) and a short 1-year USD bill ($0.2121\%$). Undiversified VaR $= \sum |x_i|V_i$.
ask: Undiversified monthly VaR of the forward is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.43m
options.why: Counted only the two bill legs and left out the EUR spot leg, which carries almost all the risk.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.8m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The spot leg alone is 4.5% of USD 123m, which is already about USD 5.6m.

options.label: ≈ USD 600m
options.why: Used the VaR percentages as decimals. That gives a VaR about five times the size of the position.

takeaway: A currency forward's VaR is almost all spot FX risk; the two interest-rate legs are rounding.

setup: Annual P/L for XYZ is normal with mean profit USD 15m and standard deviation USD 10m. Use $z_{95\%} = 1.645$ and $\mathrm{VaR} = -\mu + \sigma z$.
ask: The 95% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.44m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). $10 \times 1.645 = 16.45$ less 15 leaves about 1.45, not a few hundred thousand.

options.label: ≈ USD 16m
options.why: Dropped the mean. A USD 15m expected profit offsets almost all of the $1.645\sigma$ tail move.

options.label: ≈ USD 150m
options.why: Used the variance, $\sigma^2 = 100$, in place of $\sigma = 10$.

takeaway: A large positive mean eats most of the tail move: VaR = −μ + σz can be small, even negative.

setup: Annual P/L is normal with mean profit USD 20m and standard deviation USD 10m. You're about to compute the 5% VaR as $-\mu + \sigma z$ with $z = 1.65$, then choose between the loss reading and the profit reading.
ask: The sign of the computed VaR figure is:

options.label: Negative, so the 5% tail is still a profit
Positive, so the 5% tail is a loss
options.why: The tail move $\sigma z = 16.5$ is smaller than the USD 20m mean, so $-20 + 16.5 < 0$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The gap is USD 3.5m, a third of a standard deviation. That is clear-cut.

working.label: Reading
working.display: 5% chance that earnings fall below USD 3.5m (still a profit)

takeaway: If μ > σz, VaR is negative: read it as a minimum profit, not a loss.

setup: A USD 100 portfolio has returns with mean 10% and standard deviation 20%. Treating them as normal arithmetic returns gives a 99% VaR of $(-0.10 + 0.20 \times 2.326) \times 100 = 36.52$. Now treat the same 10% / 20% as normal geometric returns and use lognormal VaR, $P(1 - e^{\mu - \sigma z})$.
ask: Compared with 36.52, the 99% lognormal VaR:

options.label: Is higher
options.why: Exponentiating caps the loss: $1 - e^{-0.365} = 0.306$ is less than 0.365, because $1 - e^{-y} < y$ for any $y > 0$.

options.label: Is the same
options.why: The two only match for tiny moves. At $y = 0.365$ the gap between $y$ and $1 - e^{-y}$ is about 6 points.

takeaway: Lognormal VaR ≤ normal VaR for the same μ and σ: a log-return loss can never exceed 100%.

setup: Geometric returns on a USD 100 portfolio are normal with mean 10% and standard deviation 20%. Use lognormal VaR, $P_{t-1}\,(1 - e^{\mu_R - \sigma_R z})$, with $z_{95\%} = 1.645$.
ask: The 95% lognormal VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.20
options.why: Stopped at the fraction $1 - e^{-0.229} = 0.205$ and never multiplied by the USD 100 starting value.

options.label: ≈ USD 6.1
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The exponent is −0.229, so roughly a fifth of the portfolio is at risk.

options.label: ≈ USD 80
options.why: Reported $100\,e^{-0.229} = 79.5$, the value left in the tail, and forgot the $1 -$.

takeaway: Lognormal VaR ≈ P × |exponent| for small exponents, trimmed a little: −0.229 gives ≈ 20%.

setup: You estimate the 95% ES of a standard normal by slicing the 5% tail into 5 equal slices and averaging the 4 VaRs at the boundaries: 1.7507, 1.8808, 2.0537, 2.3263 (96% to 99%). Their average is 2.003.
ask: The exact ES (the limit as the number of slices grows) minus 2.003 is:

options.label: Negative: 2.003 overstates ES
options.why: The four boundaries stop at 99%; the thinnest and deepest part of the tail, beyond 2.33, is never sampled. Adding it can only raise the average.

options.label: Zero: slicing is exact
options.why: It converges only as $n \to \infty$. With $n = 5$ the estimate is 0.06 short of the true value.

takeaway: Tail-slicing ES rises toward the true value as n grows: coarse slices understate it.

setup: Expected shortfall of a standard normal ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$) at the 95% level, using $\mathrm{ES} = \mu + \sigma\,\dfrac{e^{-z^2/2}}{(1-x)\sqrt{2\pi}}$ with $z = 1.645$ and $x = 0.95$.
ask: ES is closest to:

options.why: Put the tail probability in as 5 rather than 0.05.
Stopped at the density $e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi} = 0.103$ and never divided by the tail probability. ES has to sit beyond VaR (1.645).
Dropped the $e^{-z^2/2}$ factor, i.e. used the density at 0 instead of at the quantile.

takeaway: Normal ES at 95% ≈ 2.06σ, just beyond the 1.645σ VaR. Anything below the VaR is wrong on sight.

setup: A desk's VaR is estimated from the portfolio's own historical returns (the P&L it actually earned). Today the trader adds a derivatives overlay that hedges most of the position. A second VaR uses pseudo returns: today's hedged portfolio revalued over the past.
ask: The VaR built from actual historical returns:

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is what the pseudo-return VaR does. The actual return history was earned by the unhedged book, so it cannot see today's hedge.

options.label: Rises
options.why: Nothing in the past returns changes. The hedge only lowers risk going forward, which the historical series doesn't reflect.

working.label: Historical-return VaR
working.display: Built from past P&L of the old, unhedged book: unchanged

working.label: Pseudo-return VaR
working.display: Revalues the current hedged book over history: falls

working.label: Result
working.display: Historical VaR now overstates risk (conceptual soundness failure)

takeaway: Historical-return VaR is blind to position changes; pseudo returns are what capture a new hedge.

setup: A bank puts confidence intervals around its historical-simulation VaR estimate, once in a calm period and once during a market stress period.
ask: Moving from the calm period to the stress period, the confidence interval:

options.label: Narrows
options.why: Stress scatters the tail observations, so the quantile is pinned down less precisely. The empirical finding is wider intervals.

options.label: Stays the same width
options.why: Interval width depends on how dispersed the tail observations are, and that changes sharply in stress.

working.label: Finding
working.display: Historical-simulation VaR gives wider (less precise) confidence intervals during stress periods

working.label: Contrast
working.display: More data and GARCH VaR of P&L both give tighter intervals

takeaway: Stress widens HS VaR confidence intervals; more data and GARCH P&L VaR tighten them.

setup: Model 3: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\,dw$. Short rate 5%, drift $\lambda = 0.24\%$ a year, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, $\alpha = 0.3$, one month ($dt = t = 1/12$). The monthly shock $dw$ is drawn from $N(0, \sqrt{1/12})$ and came out at 0.2.
ask: The one-month change in the short rate is closest to:

options.why: Drift only: $0.24\%/12$. The volatility term is more than ten times bigger.
Scaled $dw$ by $\sqrt{1/12}$ a second time. The draw 0.2 already comes from the monthly distribution.
Left out $dw$ and added the full $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$, as if the shock were one annual standard deviation.

takeaway: Monthly rate moves are tens of bp: the shock term dominates, and dw already carries the √dt.

setup: CIR: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$ with $r = 5\%$, $\theta = 24\%$, $k = 0.04$, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, $dt = 1/12$ and a draw $dw = 0.2$. Before adding, size the drift term against the shock term.
ask: Compared with each other, the drift and shock terms are:

options.label: Shock about 10× the drift
options.why: Took $\sqrt{5} = 2.236$ instead of $\sqrt{0.05} = 0.224$. That inflates the shock to 0.67% against a 0.063% drift.

options.label: Drift about 10× the shock
options.why: Forgot the $dt = 1/12$ on the drift. $0.04 \times 19\% = 0.76\%$ is the annual drift, not the monthly one.

takeaway: In CIR, take √r with r as a decimal; here the drift and shock come out nearly equal.

setup: CIR short-rate step: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$. Current rate 5%, long-run level 24%, $k = 0.04$, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, one month ($dt = 1/12$), random draw $dw = 0.2$.
ask: The one-month change in the short rate is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). Each term is about 0.06–0.07%, so the sum is near 0.13%.
Took $\sqrt{5}$ instead of $\sqrt{0.05}$ in the volatility term, which makes the shock ten times too big.
Plugged 24 − 5 = 19 into the drift as a whole number, then read the 0.063 result as a decimal (6.3%).

takeaway: A one-month CIR step at a 5% rate is around 13 bp; a result of 70+ bp means √5 crept in.

setup: Model 3 with $\sigma = 126$ bp and decay $\alpha = 0.025$: the short rate's instantaneous volatility $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ keeps shrinking toward zero. At a 20-year horizon the standard deviation of the terminal short rate is 4.48%.
ask: Extending the horizon from 20 to 30 years, that terminal standard deviation:

options.label: Still rises, but toward a ceiling
Falls
options.why: Falling instantaneous volatility means each extra year adds less variance, not negative variance. Cumulative uncertainty cannot shrink.

options.label: Stays flat
options.why: It only flattens in the limit ($\sigma/\sqrt{2\alpha} = 5.63\%$). At 30 years it is still well short of that.

takeaway: Decaying volatility slows the growth of terminal SD; it doesn't reverse it. SD climbs toward σ/√(2α).

setup: A mortgage pool is 5 months old and prepays at 150 PSA. The 100 PSA benchmark CPR is $0.2\% \times$ month (up to month 30), and $\mathrm{SMM} = 1 - (1 - \mathrm{CPR})^{1/12}$.
ask: The single monthly mortality (SMM) is closest to:

options.why: Converted twice: took the twelfth root of the SMM as well, so a monthly rate got de-annualized again.
Stopped at the CPR. 1.5% is the annualized rate; the question asks for the monthly one.
Multiplied the CPR by 12 instead of taking the twelfth root, which goes the wrong way.

takeaway: SMM ≈ CPR/12 in size: a 1.5% CPR means about 0.13% a month.

setup: A pool's CPR is 1.5%. You need the monthly rate. The exact route is $\mathrm{SMM} = 1 - (1 - 0.015)^{1/12}$; the shortcut is $0.015/12 = 0.125\%$.
ask: Compared with the $\mathrm{CPR}/12$ shortcut, the exact SMM is:

options.label: Slightly smaller
options.why: Survival compounds: twelve months at 0.125% each leave $(1 - 0.00125)^{12} = 0.98512$, i.e. a CPR of only 1.49%. The monthly rate must be a touch higher to reach 1.5%.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.why: Only for simple (non-compounding) rates. SMM and CPR are linked by a twelfth root, which is not linear.

takeaway: SMM from CPR is a twelfth root, not a divide-by-12; the root gives a slightly bigger monthly rate.

setup: A pool prepays at 200 PSA. The 100 PSA benchmark CPR is $0.2\% \times$ month for months 1 to 29, then 6% from month 30 onward. The pool ages from month 40 to month 60.
ask: Its CPR over that period:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Both months are past the month-30 cutoff, so the ramp no longer applies. The 200 PSA multiple scales the plateau height, not the ramp length.

options.label: Falls
options.why: PSA assumes prepayment speeds climb over the first 30 months and then level off. They don't decline with age.

takeaway: After month 30 the PSA CPR is flat: 6% × the PSA multiple, whatever the age.

setup: The one-year transition matrix gives an AAA issuer an 89.85% chance of staying AAA. Assume the matrix can be rooted to shorter horizons.
ask: The probability that an AAA issuer leaves AAA within three months is closest to:

options.why: Took the twelfth root (a one-month horizon) instead of the fourth root.
Used the one-year figure, 10.15%, without shortening the horizon.
Raised to the fourth power, which projects four years ahead instead of a quarter of a year.

takeaway: Shorter horizon → take a root of the matrix; longer → a power. A quarter-year leave rate is roughly a quarter of the annual one.

setup: An AAA issuer stays AAA over one year with probability 89.85%. For a three-month horizon the notes take the fourth root, $0.8985^{1/4}$. A shortcut would split the 10.15% annual leave rate evenly: $1 - 10.15\%/4 = 97.46\%$.
ask: Compared with the 97.46% shortcut, the fourth-root stay probability is:

options.label: Slightly higher
options.why: Staying compounds: $0.9746^4 = 0.9022$, which is above 0.8985. To end the year at 89.85% the quarterly stay probability must be a bit below 97.46%.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.why: A root is not a straight division. They only coincide when the leave rate is tiny.

takeaway: Rooting a survival probability gives a lower per-period survival than dividing the loss rate evenly.

setup: Vasicek worst-case default rate at 99.9%: $\mathrm{WCDR} = N\!\left(\dfrac{N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$. PD = 1%, so $N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) = -2.326$; $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$; correlation $\rho = 0.20$.
ask: WCDR is closest to:

options.why: Subtracted $\sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$ instead of adding it, so you get the best case rather than the worst case.
Returned the PD itself, which is the $\rho = 0$ answer. Correlation is the whole point of the stress.
Used $\rho = 0.20$ in the numerator instead of $\sqrt{\rho} = 0.447$.

takeaway: A modest ρ = 0.20 turns a 1% PD into a ~15% worst-case default rate; that is why capital is so ρ-sensitive.

setup: Building the Vasicek WCDR for PD = 1% ($N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) = -2.326$), $\rho = 0.20$ and 99.9% confidence ($N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$). First compute the numerator $N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$.
ask: The sign of that numerator is:

options.label: Positive, so WCDR is above 50%
options.why: $\sqrt{0.20} \times 3.090 = 1.38$ is not enough to offset −2.326. The numerator only turns positive when $\rho$ exceeds about 0.57.

options.label: Roughly zero
options.why: The numerator is −0.94, nearly one full unit below zero, which still leaves WCDR well under 50%.

takeaway: For low PDs the WCDR numerator stays negative, so the worst case is high but still under 50%.

setup: A loan portfolio has PD = 1% and a Vasicek correlation of $\rho = 0.20$, giving a 99.9% worst-case default rate of 14.6%. The correlation assumption is raised to 0.30, with PD and confidence level unchanged.
ask: The worst-case default rate (and so the IRB capital charge):

options.label: Falls
options.why: The numerator is negative, so the smaller $\sqrt{1-\rho}$ does push the ratio down a little. But the $\sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$ term grows much faster, and the net effect is up.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: WCDR depends directly on $\rho$. Only at $\rho = 0$ does it collapse to the PD.

takeaway: More asset correlation → fatter default-rate tail → higher WCDR and higher capital.

setup: CreditRisk+ treats the expected number of defaults $qn$ as gamma-distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, which turns the Poisson default count into a negative binomial. The analyst raises $\sigma$ and leaves $\mu$ unchanged.
ask: The probability of an extreme year with a very large number of defaults:

options.label: Falls
options.why: More uncertainty about the default rate spreads the default-count distribution, putting more mass in the right tail.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The mean number of defaults is unchanged, but the tail isn't. $\sigma$ is how CreditRisk+ builds in default correlation, and $\sigma \to 0$ recovers the thin-tailed Poisson.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Higher $\sigma$ = more uncertainty in the default rate = implied default correlation

working.label: Result
working.display: Right tail of the default-count distribution fattens: extreme outcomes more likely

takeaway: In CreditRisk+, default-rate volatility σ plays the role of correlation: raise it and the tail fattens.
